questions.prompt: How many valence electrons does a halogen atom have?
questions.explanation: Every halogen has seven valence electrons — exactly one short of a full shell of eight.
questions.misconception: One is the alkali metal count and eight is the noble gas count — the halogens sit right between, at seven, with one space to fill.

options: They are one electron short of a full shell and grab one eagerly
They have too many electrons to hold
questions.explanation: Being just one electron short of a full, stable shell, halogens grab an extra electron from almost anything — which makes them highly reactive.
questions.misconception: Weight and size don't drive reactivity here — the one-electron shortage does. That is also why fluorine, the top halogen, is the most reactive element known.

questions.prompt: When a halogen like chlorine gains one electron, what does it become?
questions.explanation: Grabbing one extra electron gives chlorine a -1 charge — a chloride ion, Cl⁻ — and a full, stable outer shell.
questions.misconception: Gaining an electron adds a NEGATIVE charge, not a positive one — so halogens form -1 anions, the mirror image of the alkali metals' +1 cations.

questions.prompt: Sodium (one extra electron) meets chlorine (one electron short). What do they build?
questions.explanation: Sodium gives its one extra electron to chlorine; the +1 sodium ion and -1 chloride ion attract and lock into table salt, NaCl.
questions.misconception: It's easy to think opposite families can't get along — but it's precisely because they are opposite (one offers an electron, one needs it) that they bond so perfectly.
